title: Line-based three-way merge
spec:
The repository is empty. Create `merge3.py` implementing a line-based three-way merge.

API:
- `merge(base, ours, theirs, style="diff3")`: each argument is a list of strings (lines without line terminators). Returns `(lines, conflicts)`: the merged list of lines and the number of conflict blocks in it. `style` is `"diff3"` or `"merge"`; anything else raises `ValueError`. The inputs must not be modified.
- `merge_text(base, ours, theirs, style="diff3")`: the same on strings. Split each text with `text.split("\n")`, merge, and return `("\n".join(lines), conflicts)`.

Algorithm (follow it exactly; the result is fully determined by it):
1. Alignment. For each side S in (ours, theirs) compute `difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, base, S, autojunk=False).get_matching_blocks()`. Base line `i` is matched to side line `j` when some block `(a, b, n)` has `a <= i < a + n` and `j = b + (i - a)`.
2. Stable lines are the base lines matched in BOTH sides. Take them in base order, add a virtual stable line before everything at positions (-1, -1, -1) and one after everything at (len(base), len(ours), len(theirs)), each stable line having a position (i, j_ours, j_theirs).
3. Between each pair of consecutive stable lines p and q there is a gap made of `B = base[p.i+1 : q.i]`, `O = ours[p.o+1 : q.o]`, `T = theirs[p.t+1 : q.t]`. Output, in order: for each gap its resolution, followed by the stable line q itself (taken from ours; nothing for the final virtual line).
4. Gap resolution, first rule that applies: if `O == T`, output O (no change, the same change on both sides, or both deleted); else if `O == B`, output T; else if `T == B`, output O; else it is a conflict.
5. Conflict, style `"diff3"`: output the lines `<<<<<<< ours`, O, `||||||| base`, B, `=======`, T, `>>>>>>> theirs`.
   Conflict, style `"merge"`: first remove the longest common prefix of O and T and output it before the conflict, then from what is left remove the longest common suffix of O and T and output it after the conflict. Between them output `<<<<<<< ours`, the rest of O, `=======`, the rest of T, `>>>>>>> theirs` (either rest may be empty; there is no base section).
   Every conflict counts as one in `conflicts`.

Consequences worth testing: edits to adjacent lines (no stable line between them) form one gap and so conflict; two sides inserting different lines at the same place conflict, but identical insertions merge cleanly; a change on one side and a deletion of the same lines on the other conflict.

Example (one line per letter): base `a b c d e`, ours `a B c d e`, theirs `a b c D e` merges to `a B c D e` with 0 conflicts; base `a b c d`, ours `a X c d`, theirs `a b Y d` gives one conflict covering lines b..c.

Inputs can have a few thousand lines; a merge must finish in under a second. Add unit tests runnable with `python3 -m unittest -q`.
acceptance: the merge follows the specified alignment, gap and resolution rules exactly
conflict blocks use the exact marker lines for both styles, with prefix/suffix trimming in merge style
merge_text splits and joins on \n and the conflict count is correct
